interactions.label: Albumin maintains oncotic pressure, the force that keeps fluid inside blood vess

params.question: Albumin maintains oncotic pressure, the force that keeps fluid inside blood vessels. If a patient's albumin level falls significantly, what is the most likely physiological consequence?

answers.text: Enhanced blood clotting due to increased fibrinogen activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fibrinogen is responsible for clotting, not albumin. A fall in albumin does not directly enhance coagulation.

answers.text: Elevated red blood cell count from bone marrow stimulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Red blood cell production is driven by erythropoietin in response to hypoxia, not by changes in albumin levels.

answers.text: Fluid leaking from blood vessels into surrounding tissues

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! When albumin falls, oncotic pressure drops and fluid leaks out of blood vessels into the interstitial space, causing oedema. This is seen clinically in nephrotic syndrome and liver cirrhosis.

answers.text: Reduced antibody production and immunodeficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Antibody production depends on gamma globulins (immunoglobulins from plasma cells), not albumin. Albumin's primary role is maintaining oncotic pressure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review albumin's function. The narration explained that oncotic pressure is 'the force that keeps fluid inside blood vessels' — think about what happens when that force weakens.
Well done! Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and its oncotic role is critical — reduced albumin causes oedema, a key clinical sign in liver and kidney disease.

params.question: In actively exercising skeletal muscle, which combination of local conditions shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT, promoting oxygen release?

answers.text: Rising temperature, rising pH, and falling CO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Rising pH (more alkaline) and falling CO₂ would shift the curve LEFT, making haemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly — the opposite of what exercising muscle needs.

answers.text: Rising temperature, falling pH, and rising CO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Exercising muscle is hot, acidic, and CO₂-rich. All three factors reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity (right shift), releasing more oxygen precisely where metabolic demand is highest. This combined effect of pH and CO₂ is called the Bohr effect.

answers.text: Falling temperature, falling pH, and rising CO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While falling pH and rising CO₂ do cause a right shift, exercising muscle generates heat — so temperature rises rather than falls.

answers.text: Falling temperature, rising pH, and falling CO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. All three of these conditions would shift the curve LEFT, causing haemoglobin to hold oxygen more tightly — the exact opposite of the right shift seen in active tissues.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: exercising muscle generates heat, produces CO₂, and lowers pH through lactic acid. These conditions all shift the curve RIGHT — the Bohr effect ensures more oxygen is released where it is needed most.
Excellent! Understanding the Bohr effect is central to haemoglobin physiology — exercising muscle creates exactly the conditions that maximise oxygen delivery.

interactions.label: When body iron stores are adequate, hepcidin levels rise, which preserves ferrop

params.question: When body iron stores are adequate, hepcidin levels rise, which preserves ferroportin on enterocyte membranes and allows continued iron absorption.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is actually false. The first part is right — adequate iron stores do raise hepcidin. But hepcidin degrades ferroportin (not preserves it), which blocks iron export from enterocytes. This is a crucial negative-feedback loop: high stores → high hepcidin → ferroportin degradation → reduced absorption.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false! While adequate iron stores do raise hepcidin, hepcidin actually degrades ferroportin rather than preserving it. By destroying ferroportin, hepcidin blocks iron export from enterocytes into the blood, effectively cutting absorption and preventing iron overload.

interactions.label: Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lungs, and microglia in

params.question: Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lungs, and microglia in the brain are all tissue-resident immune cells. Which circulating white blood cell is their common precursor?

answers.text: Neutrophils

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neutrophils are short-lived first responders that engulf bacteria by phagocytosis and die at infection sites, forming pus. They do not differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages.

answers.text: Basophils

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Basophils release histamine and heparin. Their tissue counterpart is the mast cell, not macrophages.

answers.text: Lymphocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Lymphocytes (T cells, B cells, and NK cells) coordinate adaptive and innate immunity but do not give rise to tissue macrophages.

answers.text: Monocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Monocytes are the largest WBCs, with a kidney-shaped nucleus. After leaving the bloodstream, they differentiate into organ-specific macrophages: Kupffer cells (liver), alveolar macrophages (lungs), and microglia (brain). They also serve as antigen-presenting cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the five WBC types. Monocytes are unique among leucocytes in that they leave the blood and take on new identities as tissue-resident macrophages in virtually every organ.
Well done! The monocyte-macrophage system is a key concept — a single circulating cell type populates diverse tissues with specialised immune sentinels.

interactions.label: Which pathway is considered the primary initiator of blood coagulation in the bo

params.question: Which pathway is considered the primary initiator of blood coagulation in the body, and how is it triggered?

answers.text: The intrinsic pathway, initiated by exposed collagen activating Factor XII

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The intrinsic pathway does begin with collagen activating Factor XII, but it serves as an amplification pathway rather than the primary initiator of coagulation in vivo.

answers.text: The common pathway, initiated by thrombin converting fibrinogen to fibrin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The common pathway is the final convergence point of both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. It completes clot formation but does not initiate coagulation.

answers.text: The extrinsic pathway, initiated by tissue factor released from damaged cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The extrinsic pathway is the primary initiator of coagulation. Tissue factor from damaged cells combines with Factor VII and calcium to activate Factor X. Clinically, this pathway is monitored by the prothrombin time (PT), normally eleven to sixteen seconds.

answers.text: The intrinsic pathway, initiated by tissue factor combining with Factor VII

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Tissue factor plus Factor VII describes the extrinsic pathway, not the intrinsic one. The intrinsic pathway begins with Factor XII activation by exposed collagen.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three coagulation pathways. The extrinsic pathway (tissue factor + Factor VII) is the body's primary initiator of clotting, tested by PT. The intrinsic pathway (Factor XII + collagen) amplifies it, tested by aPTT.
Excellent! Recognising the extrinsic pathway as the primary in-vivo initiator is essential. The intrinsic pathway amplifies the response, and both converge on the common pathway to form fibrin.

interactions.label: In haemolytic disease of the newborn, an Rh-negative mother's anti-D antibodies

params.question: In haemolytic disease of the newborn, an Rh-negative mother's anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and attack fetal red blood cells in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy. Which immunoglobulin class are these antibodies?

answers.text: IgG

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Anti-D antibodies are IgG, the only immunoglobulin class small enough to cross the placenta. In a sensitised Rh-negative mother, these IgG antibodies enter the fetal circulation and destroy Rh-positive red blood cells. Prevention is anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery.

answers.text: IgM

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. IgM is the class of naturally occurring ABO antibodies. It is a large pentameric molecule that cannot cross the placenta. IgM causes acute intravascular haemolysis in ABO-incompatible transfusions, not HDN.

answers.text: IgA

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. IgA is the predominant antibody in mucosal secretions such as saliva, breast milk, and intestinal fluid. It does not play a significant role in haemolytic disease of the newborn.

answers.text: IgE

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. IgE mediates allergic reactions and parasitic defence by binding mast cells and basophils, triggering histamine release — unrelated to red blood cell destruction in HDN.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: Rh antibodies are acquired (not naturally occurring) IgG antibodies. IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, making it the pathogenic class in haemolytic disease of the newborn.
Well done! IgG crossing the placenta is the key mechanism in HDN — this is precisely why anti-D prophylaxis targets the maternal immune response before IgG production ramps up.
